n: Triceps Brachii Anatomy and Clinical Relevance

faq.a: A rupture produces a palpable gap above the olecranon and inability to actively extend the elbow, whereas a strain allows some extension with pain.
faq.q: How can I tell a triceps tendon rupture from a simple muscle strain?

faq.a: It runs in the radial groove between the lateral and medial heads, so fractures or deep lacerations in this area can directly damage it.
faq.q: Why is the radial nerve most at risk in posterior arm injuries?

faq.a: Pain on passive elbow flexion with a tense, firm posterior compartment; loss of sensation distal to the injury is a late sign.
faq.q: What bedside test helps confirm compartment syndrome in the posterior arm?

exam: A patient presents after a fall with inability to extend the elbow; what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a focused exam for a tendon gap and obtain a plain elbow X‑ray to rule out avulsion fracture; if X‑ray unavailable, rely on clinical findings and arrange ultrasound.

How does radial nerve palsy alter the examination of the triceps? — Weak elbow extension and loss of wrist/finger extension indicate proximal nerve involvement; differentiate from isolated muscle injury.

What are the key features that distinguish a posterior compartment syndrome from a simple soft‑tissue bruise? — Tense swelling, pain on passive stretch, and neurovascular compromise; urgent fasciotomy is indicated.
Explain why a long‑head triceps injury may affect shoulder function. — The long head crosses the shoulder joint, contributing to extension and adduction; injury can limit overhead reaching.

In a low‑resource clinic without MRI, how would you confirm a triceps tendon rupture? — Use bedside palpation for a gap, assess active extension, and obtain an ultrasound if possible; otherwise manage based on clinical diagnosis.

What management steps are required for an acute triceps tendon rupture? — Immobilise the elbow in extension, arrange surgical repair when feasible, provide analgesia, and start early physiotherapy after healing.
Why should non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs be used cautiously in patients with suspected compartment syndrome? — NSAIDs may mask pain, delaying recognition of worsening compartment pressure.

A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy develops a posterior arm swelling; what infections should be considered? — Opportunistic bacterial cellulitis, mycobacterial abscess, or fungal infection; obtain culture and start empiric antibiotics while arranging imaging.
ai.title: Triceps Brachii Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The triceps brachii is the primary elbow extensor, composed of three heads with distinct origins and a common insertion on the olecranon. Understanding its neurovascular supply and common injuries is essential for bedside assessment and surgical planning in low‑resource settings.

b: Common insertion: olecranon process of ulna
sections.p: The triceps brachii is a large, superficial muscle of the posterior arm that extends the forearm at the elbow and stabilises the shoulder joint.

b: Long head crosses the shoulder joint
Lateral head is the most palpable when the arm is flexed
Medial head is deep and often spared in isolated injuries
sections.p: The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, the lateral head from the posterior surface of the humerus above the radial groove, and the medial head from the posterior humerus below the radial groove.

b: Radial nerve: posterior interosseous branch supplies forearm extensors
Brachial artery accompanies the nerve in the groove
sections.p: The triceps lies superficial to the humerus and deep to the skin and subcutaneous tissue. The radial nerve runs in the radial groove between the lateral and medial heads, making it vulnerable to injury.

b: Profunda brachii supplies the long and lateral heads
Medial head receives branches from the ulnar collateral artery
sections.p: Arterial branches arise from the profunda brachii artery, a deep branch of the brachial artery, and from the radial recurrent artery.

b: Sensory loss over posterior forearm suggests radial nerve injury
sections.p: All three heads are innervated by the radial nerve (C6‑C8). The long head receives fibers from the C7 root, while the lateral and medial heads receive C6‑C8 fibers.

b: Long head contributes to shoulder extension
sections.p: Primary action is elbow extension; the long head also assists in shoulder extension and adduction. It stabilises the elbow during pushing motions.

b: Isolated triceps tendon rupture: sudden pain, inability to extend elbow, palpable gap above olecranon
Radial nerve palsy: wrist drop, loss of triceps strength, sensory loss on dorsal hand
Compartment syndrome of the posterior arm: tense swelling, pain on passive stretch, requires urgent fasciotomy
sections.p: Trauma, over‑use, and nerve compression can impair triceps function. In low‑resource settings, presentations often follow falls, road‑traffic accidents, or prolonged manual labor.

t.b: Detects avulsion fracture of olecranon or bone fragments; if unavailable, rely on clinical gap and loss of extension
Identifies tendon rupture or hematoma; useful where MRI is not available
Confirms radial nerve injury severity; if unavailable, use clinical motor and sensory exam

b: Ask patient to extend elbow against resistance; weakness suggests triceps or radial nerve problem
Palpate the posterior arm for a tendon gap or swelling
Test wrist and finger extension to assess radial nerve integrity
sections.p: A focused musculoskeletal exam can differentiate triceps pathology from other elbow disorders.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive loss of elbow extension with a palpable gap
Signs of compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, tense swelling, paresthesia)
Complete radial nerve palsy with sensory loss
